opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually a really interesting question, because people tend to assume that intelligence scales almost linearly with parameter count, and that a smaller model is just a "lite" version of the bigger one. I don't fully see it that way, especially for Omni.

Pro, with more parameters, will probably still have an edge on things that depend heavily on raw knowledge capacity: long-tail facts, very deep reasoning chains in math or code, places where you simply need more memory in the weights. I'm not going to pretend that gap disappears.

But Omni is trained on a much richer signal. It sees images, hears audio, watches video, and has to tie all of that back to language. When I think about where intelligence comes from, a big part of it is grounding: understanding that words refer to things in the world, that events unfold over time, that tone of voice carries meaning text alone can't capture. A text-only model has to infer all of that indirectly from how people write about the world. An omni model gets to learn it more directly. So per parameter, I suspect the "density" of world understanding can be higher.

There's also the interaction side. Intelligence in practice isn't just answering a benchmark question. It's perceiving the situation, responding in real time, adjusting when someone interrupts you or points at something. A smaller, faster omni model may actually feel more intelligent in those settings than a larger model that's slower and only sees text.

So my view is that the two aren't really on the same axis. Pro pushes the ceiling of abstract reasoning; Omni pushes how broadly and naturally a model understands and engages with the world. Long term, I think those converge. The most capable models will be natively multimodal, and what we learn from making Omni efficient will feed directly into that. If anything, I'd say Omni's potential is underestimated precisely because people look at the parameter count first.

r001.rationale: The response says Omni may outperform Pro in some real-time, multimodal settings and that their strengths may converge long term, but it does not clearly state that Omni may approach Pro’s overall intelligence level.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you, Xiaojun. That's a question I think about a lot, because the parameter count can be misleading.

If you only look at the number of parameters, Omni is smaller than Pro, so the intuitive expectation is that it should be less intelligent. But that intuition comes from the pure text era, where scaling was almost one-dimensional: more parameters, more data, better model. Omni is a different kind of object. It's native multimodal from pre-training, so vision, audio, and text share one set of weights and one representation space from the beginning. That changes what "intelligence per parameter" means.

A few things give me confidence that Omni's ceiling is higher than its size suggests.

First, data density. Pure text data is approaching its limits, and a lot of the remaining text is low quality or redundant. Multimodal data is still largely untapped. When a model learns from images, video, speech, and text together, the signal about the physical world is much richer, and the model learns certain things, like spatial relations, causality, and timing, that text describes poorly. So a smaller model with richer supervision can learn concepts more efficiently.

Second, cross-modal transfer is real. We saw that training on vision and audio didn't just add capabilities, it sometimes improved reasoning on text tasks. That was not obvious to us in advance. It suggests the modalities regularize each other, and the model ends up with a more grounded internal world model.

Third, intelligence isn't a single scalar. Pro will stay ahead on the hardest long-chain reasoning, math, and code, where depth really does come from scale and from reinforcement learning on top of a large base. Omni's strength is a different axis: it can see, listen, and respond in real time with low latency. For a lot of real tasks, especially interacting with a person or a device, that is the more useful form of intelligence, even if the raw reasoning depth is a step behind.

So my honest view is this. On a static benchmark, Pro is stronger today, and that gap is expected. But I would not frame Omni as a "small Pro." It's a different scaling path, and over the next one or two generations I expect the architecture and the data advantages to compound. The question of which one is more intelligent will eventually depend on what you're asking the model to do, not on how many parameters it has.

r001.rationale: The response says Omni’s architecture and data advantages are expected to compound over the next generations, supporting the view that it may move closer to Pro’s level despite Pro being stronger today.

astra-6.text: I wouldn’t judge Omni’s potential intelligence by parameter count alone. A smaller model can be more efficient in how it uses its capacity, and learning across text, audio, and images could give it information that text alone doesn’t capture. But that doesn’t automatically mean it will outperform Pro in reasoning. I’d distinguish the breadth of what it can perceive and do from the depth of its reasoning, then compare them on actual tasks. A smaller parameter count is a constraint, but it isn’t enough to tell us where the ceiling is.

r001.rationale: The response says parameter count alone cannot determine Omni’s ceiling and notes possible efficiency gains, but it does not clearly express a belief that Omni may approach Pro’s intelligence level.
